title: NVIDIA’s Vera Whitepaper Has a Thread Loose
content_html:
Hello you fine Internet folks,

NVIDIA has published a 45-page whitepaper explaining Vera, its first server CPU built around the company’s own Olympus core. On paper, Vera is a fascinating chip with an 88-core monolithic compute die, Olympus being a 10-wide Arm v9.2 core that has value prediction, a graph prefetcher, 2 MB of private L2 per core, 164 MB of shared last-level cache, and eight LPDDR5X memory interfaces promising 1.2 TB/s.

Unfortunately, NVIDIA also spends a good part of the paper trying to turn those interesting design choices into a morality play about x86. Traditional simultaneous multithreading is drawn as time-slicing, a configurable NUMA topology is presented as an unavoidable 32-node maze, four SPEC components become “agentic benchmarks,” undefined performance-counter ratios are promoted as causal proof, and an unlabeled pictogram becomes a 1.8x reinforcement-learning result.

The frustrating part is that Vera does not need this help, with early independent testing suggesting Olympus is genuinely formidable. The whitepaper’s strongest case is the hardware; its weakest case is the story wrapped around it, so let’s pull that story apart.

Before getting out the cheese grater, let’s talk about the good stuff. Olympus is a very wide out-of-order Arm core.

Its front end can decode ten instructions per cycle and handle up to two taken branches per cycle. NVIDIA describes a neural branch predictor, value prediction, memory renaming, a large instruction window, six 128-bit SVE pipes, four load pipes, two store pipes, a 96 KB L1 data cache, and roughly 10-cycle access to a 2 MB private L2. Eighty-eight of those cores sit behind a 3.4 TB/s coherency fabric and a distributed 164 MB system-level cache.

Looking closer at the core, the value prediction is one of the more unique additions that Olympus has. This has been a research area for a long time and what value prediction allows Olympus to do is if the core correctly predicts a result, dependent instructions can keep moving instead of piling up behind a long-latency operation. Researchers have discovered that Apple uses value prediction in their cores and AMD talked about how in Family 17h (Zen 1 and 2) they could predict the value of some floating point instructions. However, AMD’s Family 17h implementation was quite limited, while Olympus appears to have a broader value-prediction implementation closer to Apple’s.

However, the graph prefetcher is not unique to NVIDIA. Intel has a similar mechanism called Data-Dependent Prefetcher that has been in shipping silicon since at least 2022. Intel’s newest datacenter CPU, Granite Rapids, also has an Array of Pointers prefetcher which “treats the data prefetched for a constant stride load as a pointer and may issue prefetch requests to the memory addresses corresponding to the pointer’s value.” This is fundamentally the same producer-consumer idea that NVIDIA describes for its graph prefetcher. Intel’s implementation is fairly constrained, so NVIDIA’s implementation may be able to deal with more complex chains than Intel’s implementation. So while Vera’s Graph Prefetcher may be an implementation that can deal with more workloads, producer-consumer prefetching is not a new idea.

Nor is a “neural branch predictor” a new idea. Back in 2012, AMD implemented a perceptron branch predictor in the Piledriver microarchitecture and continued to use a perceptron-based branch predictor in Zen 1. However, starting with Zen 2, AMD used a perceptron BPU only for its initial direction prediction, with a TAGE predictor overriding it because it delivered a 30% reduction in mispredictions. With Zen 5, AMD has likely fully committed to TAGE predictors, if it had not already done so with Zen 3 or Zen 4.

Moving to the SoC side, with how beefy the Olympus core is, NVIDIA has given Vera an equally beefy memory subsystem. Vera pairs eight SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X modules with up to 1.5 TB of capacity and 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth. NVIDIA claims the populated memory subsystem only consumes approximately 50 watts. A conventional EPYC or Xeon platform can offer higher-capacity DIMMs which are easier to replace, but it pays for that flexibility in board area and power.

Most importantly, we have more than NVIDIA’s results to look at. In May, Michael Larabel at Phoronix ran an early Vera system against current Arm and x86 servers. Across the NVIDIA-permitted test set, Vera’s geomean was 10% above a 5 GHz EPYC 9575F, 1.55x a Xeon 6980P, and 1.63x Grace which makes Vera the most performant Arm server CPU we have seen in public testing. There are major caveats with the testing, such as NVIDIA choosing the permitted workload scope and not allowing frequency or power monitoring. The system that Phoronix tested was pre-production and the test window was one day which puts a fairly hard limit on what they could test irrespective of the limits NVIDIA placed. This means that broader coverage will have to wait until Vera can be found in the wild rather than just in NVIDIA’s labs.

Still, the result is strong enough that we can reject the explanation that the charts in NVIDIA’s whitepaper are all fantasy. Olympus appears to be a fast CPU core, so now we can ask whether the whitepaper proves what NVIDIA says it proves.

Here is the first major technical error in the document.

Figure 5 contrasts “Traditional SMT (x86)” with NVIDIA’s Spatial Multithreading. The x86 side depicts the branch predictor, decode, execution, load/store, and memory stages alternating between two threads. The caption says Vera avoids “opportunistic time-sharing” by partitioning resources across its two hardware threads.

NVIDIA’s diagram gives a misleading impression of how SMT is usually implemented, both on x86-64 and other ISAs. SMT implementations share various stages in the execution pipeline by either selecting a thread to service every cycle, or by behaving in a thread-agnostic manner. Fetch, decode, and allocate typically service threads on a per-cycle basis, while the execute and memory access stages are thread agnostic and can service micro-ops from both threads in the same cycle. Stages that threads arbitrate for do not leave resources unused when both threads can be fed, as NVIDIA’s diagram suggests. Static partitioning and per-cycle selection would provide the same average throughput to both threads in the absence of per-thread stalls. If there are stalls, per-cycle selection can give otherwise unused throughput to the un-stalled thread.

The same idea applies to thread agnostic stages like execute and cache access. Each thread is permitted to utilize as many execution units or cache ports as it can feed. In contrast, statically partitioning resources as NVIDIA suggests could lead to one thread being compute bound and unable to use half of the core’s execution resources because they’re reserved for the other thread.

Text in NVIDIA’s paper emphasizes “determinism, isolation, and quality of service” as advantages for NVIDIA’s Spatial Multithreading approach. Performance is conspicuously not called out. QoS may be a more important consideration than throughput for NVIDIA’s target market, and Spatial Multithreading may not be a bad design point. But NVIDIA’s figure makes it look like vertical space represents time, and gives a misleading impression that Spatial Multithreading is meant to give larger performance gains than traditional SMT.

By reducing resource interference between threads, Spatial Multithreading improves determinism, isolation, and quality of service compared to traditional SMT approaches. The result is a CPU architecture that can run large numbers of concurrent agent tasks while maintaining more consistent latency and throughput. - NVIDIA’s Vera whitepaper

Vera’s actual SMT performance is unknown of course, and a lot of variables go into SMT gains besides partitioning strategies at fetch, decode, execute, and memory access. Out-of-order resources like the reorder buffer, register files, and memory ordering queues can be duplicated, statically partitioned, watermarked, or competitively shared. Partitioned structures were split between the two logical processors in multi-threaded mode and recombined for one thread in single-thread mode, which was documented in 2002. Various SMT implementations use different strategies for each structure, and those choices can have significant implications for SMT gains.

Also something to note is that it apparently takes 10,000 cycles for an Olympus core to transition back to the single-thread mode once the sibling thread on that core is done. This means that software will have to be very aware about launching a second thread on an Olympus core due to the penalties incurred not only from the partitioning scheme but also from the delay of swapping back to a single thread.

It’ll be interesting to see what strategy Vera uses to partition its out-of-order resources, and how its SMT performance compares to that of other modern cores. NVIDIA’s whitepaper gives no information on that. What it does do is present a misleading diagram that suggests traditional SMT is prone to leaving resources unused, when it may actually be better at keeping the core fed than NVIDIA’s Spatial Multithreading.

NVIDIA next tells us that a large two-socket x86 system can expose “as many as 32 NUMA domains,” while Vera presents one per socket. The number is not invented. On a many-chiplet EPYC system, an administrator can expose cache-local regions as separate NUMA nodes. If you turn every locality knob toward maximum granularity, the node count gets large.

What NVIDIA leaves out is that this is configurable with AMD’s tuning guide listing NPS4, NPS2, NPS1, and even NPS0 modes. The optional “LLC as NUMA” setting can expose each last-level-cache domain separately. So “32 NUMA nodes” is not the inevitable user experience of a chiplet CPU, it is one end of a locality-control spectrum. NVIDIA presents an optional high-granularity configuration as though it were an unavoidable reality of x86 systems.

Vera’s one domain per socket simplifies scheduling and memory placement, while multiple domains let tuned software exploit physical locality. Vera chooses the simpler presentation, and NVIDIA is free to argue that this better matches its intended software stack. But an OS-visible NUMA node is an abstraction, not a wormhole. Vera still has 88 cores, distributed cache and home nodes, memory controllers around a large die, and a packet-switched coherency fabric. A flat software topology can make those distances around the large monolithic compute die more consistent, but it cannot make them nonexistent.

The paper’s core-to-core heatmaps would be a good place to quantify that advantage. Instead, NVIDIA provides colored squares with no core identities, no minimum/median/maximum table, no distribution, and no measurement procedure. “Up to 50% lower” captures NVIDIA’s best result, not Vera’s typical behavior.

One NUMA node per socket is genuinely simpler, but the whitepaper compares it against an optional 32-domain x86 configuration and presents that edge case as the baseline. The counterpoint here is that Intel has a Mesh NoC just like Vera has. The difference really between these two setups is that the clustered setup of EPYC has high latency between clusters but within a cluster the latency is low, whereas Vera and Xeon Mesh setup has uniformly average latency; the different configurations are just engineering tradeoffs.

The benchmark section is where the whitepaper, ostensibly about a CPU, starts wearing an AI conference badge it found on the floor.

NVIDIA selects four SPEC CPU 2026 integer workloads, CPython, GCC, LLVM, and Cppcheck, and calls them “agentic benchmarks.” SPEC itself describes them as a Python interpreter, two optimizing compilers, and a C/C++ static analyzer. Those are legitimate CPU programs. They stress large instruction footprints, branch-heavy code, allocation, and dependency chains. Agents can absolutely invoke programs like them.

But they are not agents: no model is serving tokens, no agent runtime is choosing tools. No sandbox is starting, blocking on I/O, retrieving context, evaluating an answer, or feeding observations back into a policy. These workloads may be useful proxies for the code-heavy portions of an agentic pipeline. Calling them “agentic benchmarks,” however, turns that partial overlap into a claim that they represent the complete end-to-end workload.

The paper does correctly label the SPEC results as estimates, because the Vera reference hardware was not generally available at the time of the run. Figure 15 shows a 1.7x to 1.8x advantage for the four selected components, normalized per physical core under a fully loaded two-socket system. Flip to the configuration pages and the full estimated SPECrate 2026 Integer Base totals are 925 for two Vera sockets and 898 for two EPYC 9755 sockets which is a 3.0% system-throughput advantage.

Both numbers can be true. Vera uses 176 physical cores across two sockets, while the EPYC system uses 256. Divide each score by physical-core count and Vera is about 50% faster per core across the full integer-rate suite with the selected tests reaching 70 to 80%.

There is another terminology collision. NVIDIA calls Figure 19 “single thread IPC” while describing a fully loaded system.

The published configuration runs 352 copies on 176 Vera cores and 512 copies on 256 EPYC cores, two copies per physical core. Maybe NVIDIA sampled one logical thread while its sibling was active, maybe it aggregated counters and divided, the paper does not say. The SPEC results are useful, and Vera’s per-core performance is genuinely strong. However, framing those tests as agentic workloads and emphasizing normalized figures makes the advantage appear broader than the disclosed results justify.

NVIDIA attributes Olympus’s reported IPC lead to four counter groups. Depending on the selected workload, Vera supposedly achieves up to 2.3x more branch predictions per cycle, 3.5x more taken branches per cycle, 2.4x more instruction-fetch operations per cycle, and 4.3x more backend operations per cycle.

That sounds technically specific, but it is impossible to audit without the PMU event names and definitions, raw counts, sampling intervals, clock frequencies, etc. Not to mention that an Arm instruction is not the same unit of work as an x86 instruction. An internal backend operation is even less portable: one microarchitecture may split an instruction into several micro-operations while another keeps it fused.

Cross-ISA IPC can still be informative when paired with retired-work counts, clock frequencies, and code analysis. It cannot stand alone as a performance metric. Two binaries can complete the same task in the same amount of time while reporting very different IPC. For one may simply retire more instructions that are doing less work per instruction, then you have to factor in clock frequency which could be wildly different. IPC describes the behavior of the core running a piece of code, not a universal measure of useful work.

Looking at the branch predictor results, more branch predictions per cycle could indicate a capable predictor or it could also mean the Arm binary contains more branches, the benchmark moves through code faster, or NVIDIA’s event counts speculative predictions that the EPYC event does not. Higher backend operations per cycle may correlate with performance while telling us little about which feature caused it. To isolate value prediction, graph prefetching, or the neural predictor, we need on/off experiments or at least event definitions and miss rate deltas. While the IPC advantage of Vera over Turin may be real, the charts in NVIDIA’s whitepaper don’t provide enough granularity of the results to show it.

The memory section contains NVIDIA’s strongest result and one of its weakest conclusions.

Against the dual-socket EPYC 9755 system in the paper, Vera reaches roughly 1.1 TB/s in NVIDIA’s loaded-latency plot while Turin levels off near 400 GB/s. Vera also shows 12.7 GB/s per core versus 3.1 GB/s per core for Turin. Those results do not line up with our testing of Turin CPUs.

In our testing of Turin, we were able to get approximately 570 GB/s out of Turin with the 12 channel DDR5-6400 memory subsystem. This is in direct contradiction to NVIDIA’s results which top out at ~400 GB/s of memory bandwidth. This does also throw the per-core memory bandwidth numbers into dispute with the per-core bandwidth increasing to ~4.5GB/s for the EPYC 9755.

Vera still comes out ahead, but our Turin result substantially changes the size of that advantage. Comparing Vera’s roughly 1.1 TB/s against the 570 GB/s we measured gives NVIDIA a 1.9× bandwidth lead rather than the nearly 3× lead shown in the whitepaper. Revising the EPYC 9755’s per-core result from 3.1 GB/s to approximately 4.5 GB/s similarly reduces Vera’s advantage from 4.1× to roughly 2.8×. And if we look at the SKU that AMD actually puts forward as the SKU for AI head nodes, the EPYC 9575F, then the per-core result becomes 12.7 GB/s vs the 9575F’s ~9 GB/s which is about 40% improvement for Vera. Those are still good numbers for Vera, but they tell a considerably less dramatic story.

Looking at the theoretical figures, AMD lists Turin’s limit at 614 GB/s from its 12 DDR5-6400 channels. Our 570 GB/s result reaches approximately 93% of that theoretical limit. Vera’s eight LPDDR5X-9600 interfaces provide 1.2 TB/s, while NVIDIA’s measured 1.1 TB/s reaches roughly 92% of that figure. In other words, both processors convert a remarkably similar percentage of their theoretical memory bandwidth into sustained bandwidth. Vera wins because it has approximately twice the peak bandwidth of one Turin socket and fewer cores competing for it, not because Turin is unusually poor at using its available memory bandwidth.

Despite that, the whitepaper repeatedly credits Vera’s monolithic compute die while contrasting it with “traditional chiplet-based CPUs.” A monolithic die may reduce fabric traversal and improve loaded latency, but our Turin result directly weakens that explanation for the bandwidth difference. A chiplet-based EPYC 9755 reaching approximately 93% of its theoretical limit is clearly not being held back by its chiplet topology in this case. The bulk of Vera’s bandwidth advantage comes from the memory interfaces attached to the processor.

The comparison also aged almost immediately. NVIDIA published its technical blog and whitepaper on July 21, while AMD launched 6th Gen EPYC two days later. The 96-core EPYC 9686F, which is much closer to Vera’s 88-core count, provides 16 memory channels supporting DDR5-8000 or MRDIMM-12800 for 1,024 or 1,638 GB/s per socket with the top MRDIMM speed giving Venice more theoretical bandwidth than Vera both in total memory bandwidth and per-core memory bandwidth depending on what SKU you look at.

What the new EPYC specifications and our Turin testing demonstrate is narrower than NVIDIA’s claim of “3× more memory bandwidth than the latest x86 CPU” depends on a Turin result that does not represent the bandwidth we could extract from the same processor generation. Against our result, Vera delivers approximately 1.9× the total bandwidth and 2.8× the bandwidth per core, that remains an impressive platform result but it is not evidence of a bandwidth advantage for monolithic Arm processors over chiplet-based x86 CPUs.

NVIDIA reports a 2.6x PageRank advantage over EPYC 9755 and shows Vera scaling almost linearly to 32 cores while EPYC flattens to just a 10X performance increase at 32 cores. NVIDIA attributes this improvement over Turin as down to the monolithic compute die with their high-bandwidth Scalable Coherent Fabric, the 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth that Vera has, and the graph prefetcher inside the Olympus core.

However, while the paper links GAP Benchmark Suite, it omits what variables NVIDIA used which are important factors on how this test runs. The scaling plot stops at 32 cores even though the machines have 88 and 128 cores per socket. While the 2.6x result is interesting, without the variables that NVIDIA used, the result is likely irreproducible.

For the ClickHouse testing, NVIDIA links directly to Phoronix’s result where Vera led the tested processors across three passes over a 100-million-row dataset. The whitepaper’s 1.2x chart is still selective due to not using the 9575F results, but an outside tester produced the underlying result with a recognizable workload.

Then we reach Figure 24, “Vera drives 1.8x for RL training,” with the figure being a row of little completed-task squares. There is no model, environment, CPU/GPU allocation, framework, batch size, power measurement, repetition count, or error bar. We do not even know whether the squares represent samples, steps, or some random layout of tiles at NVIDIA HQ.

This is not a bad benchmark, it simply is not a benchmark at all.

The surrounding text explains why a faster CPU could improve reinforcement-learning rollouts with faster environment steps and reward computation can feed accelerators more quickly however Figure 24 does not even pretend to measure it.

After 45 pages, my position on Vera is more positive than my position on the Vera whitepaper.

Olympus looks like a serious core with a 10-wide fixed-length decoder, large private caches, value prediction, aggressive branch handling, graph-aware prefetching, and a monolithic 88-core die all being choices pointing to a very high-performance CPU core. The memory setup is no slouch either with the LPDDR5X subsystem delivering up to 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth that memory bandwidth-hungry server workloads will love, and early independent benchmarks say the silicon can cash at least some of the checks that the whitepaper writes.

However, the paper’s competitive argument is much shakier, with it mischaracterizing x86 SMT, turning an optional NUMA configuration into a default burden, relabelling standard CPU tests as agentic workloads, hiding a 3% two-socket rate lead behind 1.8x per-core bars, comparing undefined cross-ISA counters, attributing a memory-interface win to monolithic virtue, and presenting an illustration as performance data.

None of that makes Vera slow, it simply makes NVIDIA’s proof smaller than NVIDIA Marketing’s prose.

The next round of Vera testing should be straightforward. Give independent reviewers unrestricted production hardware so that we can publish frequency, package power, and wall power figures along with testing Spatial Multithreading on/off results and of course running whatever benchmark/workload we wish on Vera. If Vera is as good as its architecture suggests, those tests will be much more persuasive than drawing x86 SMT as a tiny two-lane traffic light. The way things stand, NVIDIA’s marketing risks tarnishing Vera. NVIDIA has built enough CPU here, it can stop borrowing performance from the marketing pipeline.

The difference really between these two setups is that the clustered setup of EPYC has high latency between clusters but within a cluster the latency is low, whereas Vera and Xeon Mesh setup has uniformly average latency; the different configurations are just engineering tradeoffs.The benchmark section is where the whitepaper, ostensibly about a CPU, starts wearing an AI conference badge it found on the floor.NVIDIA selects four SPEC CPU 2026 integer workloads, CPython, GCC, LLVM, and Cppcheck, and calls them “agentic benchmarks.” SPEC itself describes them as a Python interpreter, two optimizing compilers, and a C/C++ static analyzer. Those are legitimate CPU programs. They stress large instruction footprints, branch-heavy code, allocation, and dependency chains. Agents can absolutely invoke programs like them.But they are not agents: no model is serving tokens, no agent runtime is choosing tools. No sandbox is starting, blocking on I/O, retrieving context, evaluating an answer, or feeding observations back into a policy. These workloads may be useful proxies for the code-heavy portions of an agentic pipeline. Calling them “agentic benchmarks,” however, turns that partial overlap into a claim that they represent the complete end-to-end workload.The paper does correctly label the SPEC results as estimates, because the Vera reference hardware was not generally available at the time of the run. Figure 15 shows a 1.7x to 1.8x advantage for the four selected components, normalized per physical core under a fully loaded two-socket system. Flip to the configuration pages and the full estimated SPECrate 2026 Integer Base totals are 925 for two Vera sockets and 898 for two EPYC 9755 sockets which is a 3.0% system-throughput advantage.Both numbers can be true. Vera uses 176 physical cores across two sockets, while the EPYC system uses 256. Divide each score by physical-core count and Vera is about 50% faster per core across the full integer-rate suite with the selected tests reaching 70 to 80%.There is another terminology collision. NVIDIA calls Figure 19 “single thread IPC” while describing a fully loaded system.The published configuration runs 352 copies on 176 Vera cores and 512 copies on 256 EPYC cores, two copies per physical core. Maybe NVIDIA sampled one logical thread while its sibling was active, maybe it aggregated counters and divided, the paper does not say. The SPEC results are useful, and Vera’s per-core performance is genuinely strong. However, framing those tests as agentic workloads and emphasizing normalized figures makes the advantage appear broader than the disclosed results justify.NVIDIA attributes Olympus’s reported IPC lead to four counter groups. Depending on the selected workload, Vera supposedly achieves up to 2.3x more branch predictions per cycle, 3.5x more taken branches per cycle, 2.4x more instruction-fetch operations per cycle, and 4.3x more backend operations per cycle.That sounds technically specific, but it is impossible to audit without the PMU event names and definitions, raw counts, sampling intervals, clock frequencies, etc. Not to mention that an Arm instruction is not the same unit of work as an x86 instruction. An internal backend operation is even less portable: one microarchitecture may split an instruction into several micro-operations while another keeps it fused.Cross-ISA IPC can still be informative when paired with retired-work counts, clock frequencies, and code analysis. It cannot stand alone as a performance metric. Two binaries can complete the same task in the same amount of time while reporting very different IPC. For one may simply retire more instructions that are doing less work per instruction, then you have to factor in clock frequency which could be wildly different. IPC describes the behavior of the core running a piece of code, not a universal measure of useful work.Looking at the branch predictor results, more branch predictions per cycle could indicate a capable predictor or it could also mean the Arm binary contains more branches, the benchmark moves through code faster, or NVIDIA’s event counts speculative predictions that the EPYC event does not. Higher backend operations per cycle may correlate with performance while telling us little about which feature caused it. To isolate value prediction, graph prefetching, or the neural predictor, we need on/off experiments or at least event definitions and miss rate deltas. While the IPC advantage of Vera over Turin may be real, the charts in NVIDIA’s whitepaper don’t provide enough granularity of the results to show it.The memory section contains NVIDIA’s strongest result and one of its weakest conclusions.Against the dual-socket EPYC 9755 system in the paper, Vera reaches roughly 1.1 TB/s in NVIDIA’s loaded-latency plot while Turin levels off near 400 GB/s. Vera also shows 12.7 GB/s per core versus 3.1 GB/s per core for Turin. Those results do not line up with our testing of Turin CPUs.In our testing of Turin, we were able to get approximately 570 GB/s out of Turin with the 12 channel DDR5-6400 memory subsystem. This is in direct contradiction to NVIDIA’s results which top out at ~400 GB/s of memory bandwidth. This does also throw the per-core memory bandwidth numbers into dispute with the per-core bandwidth increasing to ~4.5GB/s for the EPYC 9755.Vera still comes out ahead, but our Turin result substantially changes the size of that advantage. Comparing Vera’s roughly 1.1 TB/s against the 570 GB/s we measured gives NVIDIA a 1.9× bandwidth lead rather than the nearly 3× lead shown in the whitepaper. Revising the EPYC 9755’s per-core result from 3.1 GB/s to approximately 4.5 GB/s similarly reduces Vera’s advantage from 4.1× to roughly 2.8×. And if we look at the SKU that AMD actually puts forward as the SKU for AI head nodes, the EPYC 9575F, then the per-core result becomes 12.7 GB/s vs the 9575F’s ~9 GB/s which is about 40% improvement for Vera. Those are still good numbers for Vera, but they tell a considerably less dramatic story.Looking at the theoretical figures, AMD lists Turin’s limit at 614 GB/s from its 12 DDR5-6400 channels. Our 570 GB/s result reaches approximately 93% of that theoretical limit. Vera’s eight LPDDR5X-9600 interfaces provide 1.2 TB/s, while NVIDIA’s measured 1.1 TB/s reaches roughly 92% of that figure. In other words, both processors convert a remarkably similar percentage of their theoretical memory bandwidth into sustained bandwidth. Vera wins because it has approximately twice the peak bandwidth of one Turin socket and fewer cores competing for it, not because Turin is unusually poor at using its available memory bandwidth.Despite that, the whitepaper repeatedly credits Vera’s monolithic compute die while contrasting it with “traditional chiplet-based CPUs.” A monolithic die may reduce fabric traversal and improve loaded latency, but our Turin result directly weakens that explanation for the bandwidth difference. A chiplet-based EPYC 9755 reaching approximately 93% of its theoretical limit is clearly not being held back by its chiplet topology in this case. The bulk of Vera’s bandwidth advantage comes from the memory interfaces attached to the processor.The comparison also aged almost immediately. NVIDIA published its technical blog and whitepaper on July 21, while AMD launched 6th Gen EPYC two days later. The 96-core EPYC 9686F, which is much closer to Vera’s 88-core count, provides 16 memory channels supporting DDR5-8000 or MRDIMM-12800 for 1,024 or 1,638 GB/s per socket with the top MRDIMM speed giving Venice more theoretical bandwidth than Vera both in total memory bandwidth and per-core memory bandwidth depending on what SKU you look at.What the new EPYC specifications and our Turin testing demonstrate is narrower than NVIDIA’s claim of “3× more memory bandwidth than the latest x86 CPU” depends on a Turin result that does not represent the bandwidth we could extract from the same processor generation. Against our result, Vera delivers approximately 1.9× the total bandwidth and 2.8× the bandwidth per core, that remains an impressive platform result but it is not evidence of a bandwidth advantage for monolithic Arm processors over chiplet-based x86 CPUs.NVIDIA reports a 2.6x PageRank advantage over EPYC 9755 and shows Vera scaling almost linearly to 32 cores while EPYC flattens to just a 10X performance increase at 32 cores. NVIDIA attributes this improvement over Turin as down to the monolithic compute die with their high-bandwidth Scalable Coherent Fabric, the 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth that Vera has, and the graph prefetcher inside the Olympus core.However, while the paper links GAP Benchmark Suite, it omits what variables NVIDIA used which are important factors on how this test runs. The scaling plot stops at 32 cores even though the machines have 88 and 128 cores per socket. While the 2.6x result is interesting, without the variables that NVIDIA used, the result is likely irreproducible.For the ClickHouse testing, NVIDIA links directly to Phoronix’s result where Vera led the tested processors across three passes over a 100-million-row dataset. The whitepaper’s 1.2x chart is still selective due to not using the 9575F results, but an outside tester produced the underlying result with a recognizable workload.Then we reach Figure 24, “Vera drives 1.8x for RL training,” with the figure being a row of little completed-task squares. There is no model, environment, CPU/GPU allocation, framework, batch size, power measurement, repetition count, or error bar. We do not even know whether the squares represent samples, steps, or some random layout of tiles at NVIDIA HQ.This is not a bad benchmark, it simply is not a benchmark at all.The surrounding text explains why a faster CPU could improve reinforcement-learning rollouts with faster environment steps and reward computation can feed accelerators more quickly however Figure 24 does not even pretend to measure it.After 45 pages, my position on Vera is more positive than my position on the Vera whitepaper.Olympus looks like a serious core with a 10-wide fixed-length decoder, large private caches, value prediction, aggressive branch handling, graph-aware prefetching, and a monolithic 88-core die all being choices pointing to a very high-performance CPU core. The memory setup is no slouch either with the LPDDR5X subsystem delivering up to 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth that memory bandwidth-hungry server workloads will love, and early independent benchmarks say the silicon can cash at least some of the checks that the whitepaper writes.However, the paper’s competitive argument is much shakier, with it mischaracterizing x86 SMT, turning an optional NUMA configuration into a default burden, relabelling standard CPU tests as agentic workloads, hiding a 3% two-socket rate lead behind 1.8x per-core bars, comparing undefined cross-ISA counters, attributing a memory-interface win to monolithic virtue, and presenting an illustration as performance data.None of that makes Vera slow, it simply makes NVIDIA’s proof smaller than NVIDIA Marketing’s prose.The next round of Vera testing should be straightforward. Give independent reviewers unrestricted production hardware so that we can publish frequency, package power, and wall power figures along with testing Spatial Multithreading on/off results and of course running whatever benchmark/workload we wish on Vera. If Vera is as good as its architecture suggests, those tests will be much more persuasive than drawing x86 SMT as a tiny two-lane traffic light. The way things stand, NVIDIA’s marketing risks tarnishing Vera. NVIDIA has built enough CPU here, it can stop borrowing performance from the marketing pipeline.

blocks.html_en: NVIDIA has published a 45-page whitepaper explaining Vera, its first server CPU built around the company’s own Olympus core. On paper, Vera is a fascinating chip with an 88-core monolithic compute die, Olympus being a 10-wide Arm v9.2 core that has value prediction, a graph prefetcher, 2 MB of private L2 per core, 164 MB of shared last-level cache, and eight LPDDR5X memory interfaces promising 1.2 TB/s.

blocks.html_en: Looking closer at the core, the value prediction is one of the more unique additions that Olympus has. This has been a research area for a long time and what value prediction allows Olympus to do is if the core correctly predicts a result, dependent instructions can keep moving instead of piling up behind a long-latency operation. Researchers have discovered that Apple uses value prediction in their cores and AMD talked about how in Family 17h (Zen 1 and 2) they could predict the value of some floating point instructions. However, AMD’s Family 17h implementation was quite limited, while Olympus appears to have a broader value-prediction implementation closer to Apple’s.

blocks.html_en: However, the graph prefetcher is not unique to NVIDIA. Intel has a similar mechanism called Data-Dependent Prefetcher that has been in shipping silicon since at least 2022. Intel’s newest datacenter CPU, Granite Rapids, also has an Array of Pointers prefetcher which “treats the data prefetched for a constant stride load as a pointer and may issue prefetch requests to the memory addresses corresponding to the pointer’s value.” This is fundamentally the same producer-consumer idea that NVIDIA describes for its graph prefetcher. Intel’s implementation is fairly constrained, so NVIDIA’s implementation may be able to deal with more complex chains than Intel’s implementation. So while Vera’s Graph Prefetcher may be an implementation that can deal with more workloads, producer-consumer prefetching is not a new idea.

blocks.html_en: Nor is a “neural branch predictor” a new idea. Back in 2012, AMD implemented a perceptron branch predictor in the Piledriver microarchitecture and continued to use a perceptron-based branch predictor in Zen 1. However, starting with Zen 2, AMD used a perceptron BPU only for its initial direction prediction, with a TAGE predictor overriding it because it delivered a 30% reduction in mispredictions. With Zen 5, AMD has likely fully committed to TAGE predictors, if it had not already done so with Zen 3 or Zen 4.

blocks.html_en: Most importantly, we have more than NVIDIA’s results to look at. In May, Michael Larabel at Phoronix ran an early Vera system against current Arm and x86 servers. Across the NVIDIA-permitted test set, Vera’s geomean was 10% above a 5 GHz EPYC 9575F, 1.55x a Xeon 6980P, and 1.63x Grace which makes Vera the most performant Arm server CPU we have seen in public testing. There are major caveats with the testing, such as NVIDIA choosing the permitted workload scope and not allowing frequency or power monitoring. The system that Phoronix tested was pre-production and the test window was one day which puts a fairly hard limit on what they could test irrespective of the limits NVIDIA placed. This means that broader coverage will have to wait until Vera can be found in the wild rather than just in NVIDIA’s labs.

blocks.html_en: NVIDIA’s diagram gives a misleading impression of how SMT is usually implemented, both on x86-64 and other ISAs. SMT implementations share various stages in the execution pipeline by either selecting a thread to service every cycle, or by behaving in a thread-agnostic manner. Fetch, decode, and allocate typically service threads on a per-cycle basis, while the execute and memory access stages are thread agnostic and can service micro-ops from both threads in the same cycle. Stages that threads arbitrate for do not leave resources unused when both threads can be fed, as NVIDIA’s diagram suggests. Static partitioning and per-cycle selection would provide the same average throughput to both threads in the absence of per-thread stalls. If there are stalls, per-cycle selection can give otherwise unused throughput to the un-stalled thread.

sentences.zh: NVIDIA 的图表对于 SMT 在 x86-64 和其他 ISA 上的通常实现方式给出了误导性的印象。

sentences.zh: 获取、解码和分配通常在每个周期的基础上为线程提供服务，而执行和内存访问阶段与线程无关，并且可以在同一周期中为来自两个线程的微操作提供服务。

sentences.en: Stages that threads arbitrate for do not leave resources unused when both threads can be fed, as NVIDIA’s diagram suggests.
sentences.zh: 正如 NVIDIA 的图表所示，当两个线程都可以供电时，线程仲裁的阶段不会留下未使用的资源。

sentences.en: Static partitioning and per-cycle selection would provide the same average throughput to both threads in the absence of per-thread stalls.
sentences.zh: 在没有每线程停顿的情况下，静态分区和每周期选择将为两个线程提供相同的平均吞吐量。

sentences.zh: 如果存在停顿，则每个周期的选择可以为未停顿的线程提供原本未使用的吞吐量。

blocks.html_en: Vera’s actual SMT performance is unknown of course, and a lot of variables go into SMT gains besides partitioning strategies at fetch, decode, execute, and memory access. Out-of-order resources like the reorder buffer, register files, and memory ordering queues can be duplicated, statically partitioned, watermarked, or competitively shared. Partitioned structures were split between the two logical processors in multi-threaded mode and recombined for one thread in single-thread mode, which was documented in 2002. Various SMT implementations use different strategies for each structure, and those choices can have significant implications for SMT gains.

sentences.en: Vera’s actual SMT performance is unknown of course, and a lot of variables go into SMT gains besides partitioning strategies at fetch, decode, execute, and memory access.

blocks.html_en: Also something to note is that it apparently takes 10,000 cycles for an Olympus core to transition back to the single-thread mode once the sibling thread on that core is done. This means that software will have to be very aware about launching a second thread on an Olympus core due to the penalties incurred not only from the partitioning scheme but also from the delay of swapping back to a single thread.

blocks.html_en: NVIDIA next tells us that a large two-socket x86 system can expose “as many as 32 NUMA domains,” while Vera presents one per socket. The number is not invented. On a many-chiplet EPYC system, an administrator can expose cache-local regions as separate NUMA nodes. If you turn every locality knob toward maximum granularity, the node count gets large.

sentences.en: NVIDIA next tells us that a large two-socket x86 system can expose “as many as 32 NUMA domains,” while Vera presents one per socket.
sentences.zh: NVIDIA 接下来告诉我们，大型双插槽 x86 系统可以公开“多达 32 个 NUMA 域”，而 Vera 则为每个插槽提供一个域。

sentences.en: The number is not invented.
sentences.zh: 这个数字不是发明的。

sentences.en: On a many-chiplet EPYC system, an administrator can expose cache-local regions as separate NUMA nodes.
sentences.zh: 在多芯片 EPYC 系统上，管理员可以将缓存本地区域公开为单独的 NUMA 节点。

sentences.en: If you turn every locality knob toward maximum granularity, the node count gets large.
sentences.zh: 如果将每个位置旋钮调至最大粒度，节点数就会变大。

blocks.html_en: What NVIDIA leaves out is that this is configurable with AMD’s tuning guide listing NPS4, NPS2, NPS1, and even NPS0 modes. The optional “LLC as NUMA” setting can expose each last-level-cache domain separately. So “32 NUMA nodes” is not the inevitable user experience of a chiplet CPU, it is one end of a locality-control spectrum. NVIDIA presents an optional high-granularity configuration as though it were an unavoidable reality of x86 systems.

sentences.en: What NVIDIA leaves out is that this is configurable with AMD’s tuning guide listing NPS4, NPS2, NPS1, and even NPS0 modes.
sentences.zh: NVIDIA 遗漏的是，这可以通过 AMD 的调整指南进行配置，其中列出了 NPS4、NPS2、NPS1 甚至 NPS0 模式。

sentences.en: The optional “LLC as NUMA” setting can expose each last-level-cache domain separately.
sentences.zh: 可选的“LLC as NUMA”设置可以单独公开每个最后一级缓存域。

sentences.en: So “32 NUMA nodes” is not the inevitable user experience of a chiplet CPU, it is one end of a locality-control spectrum.
sentences.zh: 因此，“32 个 NUMA 节点”并不是小芯片 CPU 不可避免的用户体验，它只是局部控制范围的一端。

sentences.en: NVIDIA presents an optional high-granularity configuration as though it were an unavoidable reality of x86 systems.
sentences.zh: NVIDIA 提供了可选的高粒度配置，就好像它是 x86 系统不可避免的现实一样。

blocks.html_en: Vera’s one domain per socket simplifies scheduling and memory placement, while multiple domains let tuned software exploit physical locality. Vera chooses the simpler presentation, and NVIDIA is free to argue that this better matches its intended software stack. But an OS-visible NUMA node is an abstraction, not a wormhole. Vera still has 88 cores, distributed cache and home nodes, memory controllers around a large die, and a packet-switched coherency fabric. A flat software topology can make those distances around the large monolithic compute die more consistent, but it cannot make them nonexistent.

sentences.en: Vera’s one domain per socket simplifies scheduling and memory placement, while multiple domains let tuned software exploit physical locality.
sentences.zh: Vera 的每个套接字一个域简化了调度和内存布局，而多个域则让经过调整的软件可以利用物理位置。

sentences.en: Vera chooses the simpler presentation, and NVIDIA is free to argue that this better matches its intended software stack.
sentences.zh: Vera 选择了更简单的演示，NVIDIA 可以自由地辩称这更符合其预期的软件堆栈。

sentences.en: But an OS-visible NUMA node is an abstraction, not a wormhole.

sentences.zh: 扁平软件拓扑可以使大型单片计算芯片周围的距离更加一致，但不能使它们不存在。

blocks.html_en: The paper’s core-to-core heatmaps would be a good place to quantify that advantage. Instead, NVIDIA provides colored squares with no core identities, no minimum/median/maximum table, no distribution, and no measurement procedure. “Up to 50% lower” captures NVIDIA’s best result, not Vera’s typical behavior.

sentences.zh: 相反，NVIDIA 提供了没有核心标识、没有最小值/中值/最大值表、没有分布、也没有测量程序的彩色方块。

blocks.html_en: One NUMA node per socket is genuinely simpler, but the whitepaper compares it against an optional 32-domain x86 configuration and presents that edge case as the baseline. The counterpoint here is that Intel has a Mesh NoC just like Vera has. The difference really between these two setups is that the clustered setup of EPYC has high latency between clusters but within a cluster the latency is low, whereas Vera and Xeon Mesh setup has uniformly average latency; the different configurations are just engineering tradeoffs.

sentences.en: One NUMA node per socket is genuinely simpler, but the whitepaper compares it against an optional 32-domain x86 configuration and presents that edge case as the baseline.
sentences.zh: 每个插槽一个 NUMA 节点确实更简单，但白皮书将其与可选的 32 域 x86 配置进行了比较，并将该边缘情况作为基准。

sentences.en: The counterpoint here is that Intel has a Mesh NoC just like Vera has.

sentences.en: The difference really between these two setups is that the clustered setup of EPYC has high latency between clusters but within a cluster the latency is low, whereas Vera and Xeon Mesh setup has uniformly average latency; the different configurations are just engineering tradeoffs.
sentences.zh: 这两种设置之间的真正区别在于，EPYC 的集群设置在集群之间具有较高的延迟，但在集群内延迟较低，而 Vera 和 Xeon Mesh 设置具有统一的平均延迟；不同的配置只是工程上的权衡。

blocks.html_en: The benchmark section is where the whitepaper, ostensibly about a CPU, starts wearing an AI conference badge it found on the floor.

blocks.html_en: NVIDIA selects four SPEC CPU 2026 integer workloads, CPython, GCC, LLVM, and Cppcheck, and calls them “agentic benchmarks.” SPEC itself describes them as a Python interpreter, two optimizing compilers, and a C/C++ static analyzer. Those are legitimate CPU programs. They stress large instruction footprints, branch-heavy code, allocation, and dependency chains. Agents can absolutely invoke programs like them.

blocks.html_en: But they are not agents: no model is serving tokens, no agent runtime is choosing tools. No sandbox is starting, blocking on I/O, retrieving context, evaluating an answer, or feeding observations back into a policy. Calling them “agentic benchmarks,” however, turns that partial overlap into a claim that they represent the complete end-to-end workload.

sentences.en: But they are not agents: no model is serving tokens, no agent runtime is choosing tools.

blocks.html_en: The paper does correctly label the SPEC results as estimates, because the Vera reference hardware was not generally available at the time of the run. Figure 15 shows a 1.7x to 1.8x advantage for the four selected components, normalized per physical core under a fully loaded two-socket system. Flip to the configuration pages and the full estimated SPECrate 2026 Integer Base totals are 925 for two Vera sockets and 898 for two EPYC 9755 sockets which is a 3.0% system-throughput advantage.

sentences.en: An internal backend operation is even less portable: one microarchitecture may split an instruction into several micro-operations while another keeps it fused.

blocks.html_en: Cross-ISA IPC can still be informative when paired with retired-work counts, clock frequencies, and code analysis. It cannot stand alone as a performance metric. blocks.html_en: Looking at the branch predictor results, more branch predictions per cycle could indicate a capable predictor or it could also mean the Arm binary contains more branches, the benchmark moves through code faster, or NVIDIA’s event counts speculative predictions that the EPYC event does not. To isolate value prediction, graph prefetching, or the neural predictor, we need on/off experiments or at least event definitions and miss rate deltas. sentences.en: In our testing of Turin, we were able to get approximately 570 GB/s out of Turin with the 12 channel DDR5-6400 memory subsystem.
sentences.zh: 在我们对都灵的测试中，我们能够使用 12 通道 DDR5-6400 内存子系统从都灵获得大约 570 GB/s 的速度。

sentences.en: This is in direct contradiction to NVIDIA’s results which top out at ~400 GB/s of memory bandwidth.

blocks.html_en: Vera still comes out ahead, but our Turin result substantially changes the size of that advantage. Comparing Vera’s roughly 1.1 TB/s against the 570 GB/s we measured gives NVIDIA a 1.9× bandwidth lead rather than the nearly 3× lead shown in the whitepaper. Revising the EPYC 9755’s per-core result from 3.1 GB/s to approximately 4.5 GB/s similarly reduces Vera’s advantage from 4.1× to roughly 2.8×. And if we look at the SKU that AMD actually puts forward as the SKU for AI head nodes, the EPYC 9575F, then the per-core result becomes 12.7 GB/s vs the 9575F’s ~9 GB/s which is about 40% improvement for Vera. sentences.zh: 对于维拉来说，这些数字仍然不错，但它们讲述的故事却没有那么戏剧化。

blocks.html_en: Looking at the theoretical figures, AMD lists Turin’s limit at 614 GB/s from its 12 DDR5-6400 channels. Our 570 GB/s result reaches approximately 93% of that theoretical limit. Vera’s eight LPDDR5X-9600 interfaces provide 1.2 TB/s, while NVIDIA’s measured 1.1 TB/s reaches roughly 92% of that figure. In other words, both processors convert a remarkably similar percentage of their theoretical memory bandwidth into sustained bandwidth. Vera wins because it has approximately twice the peak bandwidth of one Turin socket and fewer cores competing for it, not because Turin is unusually poor at using its available memory bandwidth.

sentences.en: Looking at the theoretical figures, AMD lists Turin’s limit at 614 GB/s from its 12 DDR5-6400 channels.

sentences.zh: Vera 获胜是因为它的峰值带宽大约是 Turin 插槽的两倍，并且与之竞争的核心更少，而不是因为 Turin 在使用其可用内存带宽方面异常糟糕。

blocks.html_en: Despite that, the whitepaper repeatedly credits Vera’s monolithic compute die while contrasting it with “traditional chiplet-based CPUs.” A monolithic die may reduce fabric traversal and improve loaded latency, but our Turin result directly weakens that explanation for the bandwidth difference. The bulk of Vera’s bandwidth advantage comes from the memory interfaces attached to the processor.

blocks.html_en: Olympus looks like a serious core with a 10-wide fixed-length decoder, large private caches, value prediction, aggressive branch handling, graph-aware prefetching, and a monolithic 88-core die all being choices pointing to a very high-performance CPU core. The memory setup is no slouch either with the LPDDR5X subsystem delivering up to 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth that memory bandwidth-hungry server workloads will love, and early independent benchmarks say the silicon can cash at least some of the checks that the whitepaper writes.

content_html_zh:
各位优秀的互联网人，大家好：

NVIDIA 发布了一份长达 45 页的白皮书，解释了 Vera，这是其首款围绕该公司自己的 Olympus 内核构建的服务器 CPU。 从纸面上看，Vera 是一款令人着迷的芯片，具有 88 核单片计算芯片，Olympus 是 10 宽 Arm v9.2 核心，具有值预测、图形预取器、每个核心 2 MB 私有 L2、164 MB 共享末级缓存以及 8 个 LPDDR5X 内存接口，有望达到 1.2 TB/s。

不幸的是，NVIDIA 还花了很大一部分篇幅试图将这些有趣的设计选择变成关于 x86 的道德剧。 传统的同时多线程被绘制为时间切片，可配置的 NUMA 拓扑被呈现为不可避免的 32 节点迷宫，四个 SPEC 组件成为“代理基准”，未定义的性能计数器比率被提升为因果证明，未标记的象形图成为 1.8 倍的强化学习结果。

令人沮丧的是，维拉不需要这种帮助，早期的独立测试表明奥林巴斯确实很强大。 白皮书最有力的案例是硬件；它最薄弱的情况是围绕它的故事，所以让我们把这个故事拆开。

在拿出奶酪刨丝器之前，让我们先谈谈好东西。 Olympus 是一个非常广泛的乱序 Arm 核心。

其前端每个周期可以解码十条指令，并且每个周期最多处理两个已采取的分支。 NVIDIA 描述了一个神经分支预测器、值预测、内存重命名、一个大指令窗口、6 个 128 位 SVE 管道、4 个加载管道、2 个存储管道、一个 96 KB L1 数据缓存以及对 2 MB 私有 L2 的大约 10 个周期访问。 其中 88 个核心位于 3.4 TB/s 一致性结构和分布式 164 MB 系统级缓存后面。

仔细观察核心，价值预测是奥林巴斯更独特的附加功能之一。 长期以来，这一直是一个研究领域，价值预测允许奥林巴斯做的是，如果核心正确预测结果，相关指令可以继续移动，而不是在长延迟操作后面堆积。 研究人员发现，Apple 在其核心中使用了值预测，而 AMD 则谈到了如何在 Family 17h（Zen 1 和 2）中预测某些浮点指令的值。 然而，AMD 的 Family 17h 实施相当有限，而奥林巴斯似乎有更广泛的价值预测实施，更接近苹果。

然而，图形预取器并不是 NVIDIA 独有的。 英特尔有一个类似的机制，称为“数据相关预取器”，至少从 2022 年起就已经在出货芯片中。 英特尔最新的数据中心 CPU Granite Rapids 也有一个指针数组预取器，它“将恒定步幅负载预取的数据视为指针，并可能向与指针值相对应的内存地址发出预取请求。” 这与 NVIDIA 为其图形预取器描述的生产者-消费者理念基本相同。 英特尔的实现相当有限，因此 NVIDIA 的实现可能能够处理比英特尔的实现更复杂的链。 因此，虽然 Vera 的 Graph Prefetcher 可能是一种可以处理更多工作负载的实现，但生产者-消费者预取并不是一个新想法。

“神经分支预测器”也不是一个新想法。 早在 2012 年，AMD 在 Piledriver 微架构中实现了感知器分支预测器，并在 Zen 1 中继续使用基于感知器的分支预测器。 然而，从 Zen 2 开始，AMD 仅使用感知器 BPU 进行初始方向预测，并用 TAGE 预测器覆盖它，因为它使错误预测减少了 30%。 在 Zen 5 中，AMD 可能已经完全致力于 TAGE 预测器，如果它还没有在 Zen 3 或 Zen 4 中这样做的话。

转向 SoC 方面，凭借 Olympus 核心的强大性能，NVIDIA 为 Vera 提供了同样强大的内存子系统。 Vera 将八个 SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X 模块配对，容量高达 1.5 TB，带宽高达 1.2 TB/s。 NVIDIA 声称填充的内存子系统仅消耗大约 50 瓦。 传统的 EPYC（霄龙）或 Xeon（至强）平台可以提供更容易更换的更高容量的 DIMM，但它需要付出电路板面积和功耗方面的灵活性的代价。

最重要的是，我们可以看到的不仅仅是 NVIDIA 的结果。 五月份，Ph​​oronix 的 Michael Larabel 在当前的 Arm 和 x86 服务器上运行了早期的 Vera 系统。 在 NVIDIA 允许的测试集中，Vera 的 geomean 比 5 GHz EPYC 9575F 高出 10%，比 Xeon 6980P 高出 1.55 倍，而 Grace 则高出 1.63 倍，这使得 Vera 成为我们在公开测试中见过的性能最高的 Arm 服务器 CPU。 测试中有一些重要的注意事项，例如 NVIDIA 选择允许的工作负载范围并且不允许频率或功率监控。 Phoronix 测试的系统是预生产的，测试窗口是一天，这对他们可以测试的内容设置了相当严格的限制，无论 NVIDIA 设置了多少限制。 这意味着更广泛的覆盖范围必须等到 Vera 在野外被发现，而不仅仅是在 NVIDIA 实验室中被发现。

尽管如此，结果仍然足够强大，以至于我们可以拒绝 NVIDIA 白皮书中的图表都是幻想的解释。 奥林巴斯似乎是一个快速的CPU核心，所以现在我们可以问白皮书是否证明了NVIDIA所说的证明。

这是文档中的第一个重大技术错误。

图 5 将“传统 SMT (x86)”与 NVIDIA 的空间多线程进行了对比。 x86 方面描述了两个线程之间交替的分支预测器、解码、执行、加载/存储和内存阶段。 标题称 Vera 通过在两个硬件线程之间划分资源来避免“机会主义分时”。

NVIDIA 的图表对于 SMT 在 x86-64 和其他 ISA 上的通常实现方式给出了误导性的印象。 SMT 实现通过选择一个线程来服务每个周期，或者以与线程无关的方式运行，从而共享执行管道中的各个阶段。 获取、解码和分配通常在每个周期的基础上为线程提供服务，而执行和内存访问阶段与线程无关，并且可以在同一周期中为来自两个线程的微操作提供服务。 正如 NVIDIA 的图表所示，当两个线程都可以供电时，线程仲裁的阶段不会留下未使用的资源。 在没有每线程停顿的情况下，静态分区和每周期选择将为两个线程提供相同的平均吞吐量。 如果存在停顿，则每个周期的选择可以为未停顿的线程提供原本未使用的吞吐量。

同样的想法也适用于与线程无关的阶段，例如执行和缓存访问。 每个线程都可以使用尽可能多的执行单元或缓存端口。 相比之下，按照 NVIDIA 建议的方式静态划分资源可能会导致一个线程受到计算限制，并且无法使用一半的核心执行资源，因为这些资源是为另一个线程保留的。

NVIDIA 论文中的文字强调“确定性、隔离性和服务质量”是 NVIDIA 空间多线程方法的优势。 性能显然没有被提及。 对于 NVIDIA 的目标市场来说，QoS 可能是比吞吐量更重要的考虑因素，而空间多线程可能是一个不错的设计点。 但 NVIDIA 的数字让它看起来像是垂直空间代表时间，并给人一种误导性的印象，即空间多线程旨在比传统 SMT 提供更大的性能提升。

与传统的 SMT 方法相比，空间多线程通过减少线程之间的资源干扰，提高了确定性、隔离性和服务质量。 其结果是 CPU 架构可以运行大量并发代理任务，同时保持更一致的延迟和吞吐量。 - NVIDIA 的 Vera 白皮书

当然，Vera 的实际 SMT 性能尚不清楚，除了获取、解码、执行和内存访问的分区策略之外，SMT 增益还有很多变量。 无序资源（例如重新排序缓冲区、寄存器文件和内存排序队列）可以被复制、静态分区、加水印或竞争共享。 分区结构在多线程模式下在两个逻辑处理器之间分割，并在单线程模式下重新组合为一个线程，该记录于 2002 年记录。 各种 SMT 实施对每种结构使用不同的策略，这些选择可能对 SMT 收益产生重大影响。

另外值得注意的是，一旦该核心上的同级线程完成，奥林巴斯核心显然需要 10,000 个周期才能转换回单线程模式。 这意味着软件必须非常注意在 Olympus 核心上启动第二个线程，因为不仅会因分区方案而产生损失，而且还会因交换回单个线程的延迟而产生损失。

看看 Vera 使用什么策略来划分其无序资源，以及它的 SMT 性能与其他现代内核的性能相比如何，将会很有趣。 NVIDIA 的白皮书没有提供这方面的信息。 它的作用是提供一个误导性的图表，表明传统的 SMT 很容易导致资源闲置，而实际上它可能比 NVIDIA 的空间多线程更能保持核心的运行。

NVIDIA 接下来告诉我们，大型双插槽 x86 系统可以公开“多达 32 个 NUMA 域”，而 Vera 则为每个插槽提供一个域。 这个数字不是发明的。 在多芯片 EPYC 系统上，管理员可以将缓存本地区域公开为单独的 NUMA 节点。 如果将每个位置旋钮调至最大粒度，节点数就会变大。

NVIDIA 遗漏的是，这可以通过 AMD 的调整指南进行配置，其中列出了 NPS4、NPS2、NPS1 甚至 NPS0 模式。 可选的“LLC as NUMA”设置可以单独公开每个最后一级缓存域。 因此，“32 个 NUMA 节点”并不是小芯片 CPU 不可避免的用户体验，它只是局部控制范围的一端。 NVIDIA 提供了可选的高粒度配置，就好像它是 x86 系统不可避免的现实一样。

Vera 的每个套接字一个域简化了调度和内存布局，而多个域则让经过调整的软件可以利用物理位置。 Vera 选择了更简单的演示，NVIDIA 可以自由地辩称这更符合其预期的软件堆栈。 但操作系统可见的 NUMA 节点是一个抽象概念，而不是虫洞。 Vera 仍然拥有 88 个核心、分布式缓存和主节点、围绕大芯片的内存控制器以及数据包交换一致性结构。 扁平软件拓扑可以使大型单片计算芯片周围的距离更加一致，但不能使它们不存在。

该论文的核心到核心热图将是量化这一优势的好地方。 相反，NVIDIA 提供了没有核心标识、没有最小值/中值/最大值表、没有分布、也没有测量程序的彩色方块。 “最多降低 50%”代表的是 NVIDIA 的最佳结果，而不是 Vera 的典型行为。

每个插槽一个 NUMA 节点确实更简单，但白皮书将其与可选的 32 域 x86 配置进行了比较，并将该边缘情况作为基准。 与之相对的是，Intel 也有一个像 Vera 一样的 Mesh NoC。 这两种设置之间的真正区别在于，EPYC 的集群设置在集群之间具有较高的延迟，但在集群内延迟较低，而 Vera 和 Xeon Mesh 设置具有统一的平均延迟；不同的配置只是工程上的权衡。

在基准测试部分，白皮书表面上是关于 CPU 的，但它开始佩戴在地板上发现的人工智能会议徽章。

NVIDIA 选择了四种 SPEC CPU 2026 整数工作负载：CPython、GCC、LLVM 和 Cppcheck，并将它们称为“代理基准测试”。 SPEC 本身将它们描述为一个 Python 解释器、两个优化编译器和一个 C/C++ 静态分析器。 这些是合法的CPU 程序。 它们强调大的指令占用、大量分支的代码、分配和依赖链。 代理绝对可以调用像它们这样的程序。

但它们不是代理：没有模型提供令牌，没有代理运行时选择工具。 没有沙箱启动、阻止 I/O、检索上下文、评估答案或将观察结果反馈到策略中。 这些工作负载可能是代理管道中代码密集部分的有用代理。 然而，将它们称为“代理基准”会将部分重叠变成声称它们代表完整的端到端工作负载。

该论文确实将 SPEC 结果正确地标记为估计值，因为 Vera 参考硬件在运行时通常不可用。 图 15 显示了四个选定组件的 1.7 倍至 1.8 倍优势，在满载的双插槽系统下按每个物理核心进行标准化。 翻到配置页面，两个 Vera 插槽的完整估计 SPECrate 2026 Integer Base 总数为 925，两个 EPYC 9755 插槽为 898，系统吞吐量优势为 3.0%。

这两个数字都可能是真的。 Vera 在两个插槽上使用 176 个物理核心，而 EPYC 系统使用 256 个。 将每个分数除以物理核心数量，Vera 在整个整数速率套件中每个核心的速度提高了约 50%，所选测试达到 70% 至 80%。

还有另一个术语冲突。 NVIDIA 在描述满载系统时将图 19 称为“单线程 IPC”。

已发布的配置在 176 个 Vera 核心上运行 352 个副本，在 256 个 EPYC 核心上运行 512 个副本，每个物理核心两个副本。 也许 NVIDIA 在其同级线程处于活动状态时对一个逻辑线程进行了采样，也许它聚合了计数器并进行了划分，论文没有说明。 SPEC 结果很有用，Vera 的每核性能确实很强。 然而，将这些测试视为代理工作负载并强调标准化数字，使得优势看起来比披露的结果所证明的更广泛。

NVIDIA 将奥林巴斯报告的 IPC 领先优势归因于四个计数器组。 根据所选的工作负载，Vera 据称每个周期的分支预测数量增加了 2.3 倍，每个周期的分支预测数量增加了 3.5 倍，每个周期的取指令操作数量增加了 2.4 倍，每个周期的后端操作数量增加了 4.3 倍。

这听起来在技术上很具体，但如果没有 PMU 事件名称和定义、原始计数、采样间隔、时钟频率等，就不可能进行审核。更不用说 Arm 指令与 x86 指令不是同一工作单元。 内部后端操作的可移植性甚至更差：一种微体系结构可能会将一条指令拆分为多个微操作，而另一种微体系结构则将其保持融合。

当与退役工作计数、时钟频率和代码分析结合使用时，跨 ISA IPC 仍然可以提供丰富的信息。 它不能单独作为性能指标。 两个二进制文件可以在相同的时间内完成相同的任务，同时报告截然不同的 IPC。 因为可能会简单地淘汰更多指令，而每条指令执行的工作量更少，那么您必须考虑可能截然不同的时钟频率。 IPC 描述了运行一段代码的核心的行为，而不是有用工作的通用衡量标准。

查看分支预测器结果，每个周期更多的分支预测可能表明预测器功能强大，或者也可能意味着 Arm 二进制文件包含更多分支，基准测试在代码中移动得更快，或者 NVIDIA 的事件计数了 EPYC 事件没有的推测性预测。 每个周期更高的后端操作可能与性能相关，但很少告诉我们是哪个功能导致的。 为了隔离值预测、图预取或神经预测器，我们需要开/关实验或至少需要事件定义和丢失率增量。 虽然 Vera 相对于 Turin 的 IPC 优势可能是真实的，但 NVIDIA 白皮书中的图表并未提供足够详细的结果来显示这一优势。

内存部分包含 NVIDIA 最强的结果和最弱的结论之一。

与本文中的双插槽 EPYC 9755 系统相比，Vera 在 NVIDIA 的加载延迟图中达到了大约 1.1 TB/s，而 Turin 则稳定在接近 400 GB/s。 Vera 还显示每核心 12.7 GB/s，而 Turin 每核心 3.1 GB/s。 这些结果与我们对 Turin CPU 的测试不符。

在我们对都灵的测试中，我们能够使用 12 通道 DDR5-6400 内存子系统从都灵获得大约 570 GB/s 的速度。 这与 NVIDIA 的结果直接矛盾，NVIDIA 的内存带宽最高可达约 400 GB/s。 这也确实引发了每核心内存带宽数字的争议，EPYC 9755 的每核心带宽增加到约 4.5GB/s。

维拉仍然领先，但我们都灵的结果大大改变了这一优势的大小。 将 Vera 的大约 1.1 TB/s 与我们测得的 570 GB/s 进行比较，NVIDIA 的带宽领先 1.9 倍，而不是白皮书中显示的近 3 倍。 将 EPYC 9755 的每核结果从 3.1 GB/s 修改为大约 4.5 GB/s，同样会将 Vera 的优势从 4.1 倍降低到大约 2.8 倍。 如果我们看看 AMD 实际上提出的作为 AI 头节点 SKU 的 SKU（EPYC 9575F），那么每核结果将变为 12.7 GB/s，而 9575F 的约为 9 GB/s，这对于 Vera 来说大约提高了 40%。 对于维拉来说，这些数字仍然不错，但它们讲述的故事却没有那么戏剧化。

从理论数据来看，AMD 将 Turin 的 12 个 DDR5-6400 通道的限制限制为 614 GB/s。 我们的 570 GB/s 结果达到了理论极限的大约 93%。 Vera 的 8 个 LPDDR5X-9600 接口提供 1.2 TB/s，而 NVIDIA 测得的 1.1 TB/s 大约达到该数字的 92%。 换句话说，两个处理器将其理论内存带宽的百分比非常相似地转换为持续带宽。 Vera 获胜是因为它的峰值带宽大约是 Turin 插槽的两倍，并且与之竞争的核心更少，而不是因为 Turin 在使用其可用内存带宽方面异常糟糕。

尽管如此，白皮书还是反复赞扬了 Vera 的单片计算芯片，同时将其与“传统的基于小芯片的 CPU”进行了对比。 单片芯片可能会减少结构遍历并改善加载延迟，但我们的都灵结果直接削弱了对带宽差异的解释。 在这种情况下，基于小芯片的 EPYC 9755 达到其理论极限的约 93% 显然不会受到其小芯片拓扑的阻碍。 Vera 的大部分带宽优势来自连接到处理器的内存接口。

对比几乎立刻就变老了。 NVIDIA 于 7 月 21 日发布了技术博客和白皮书，而 AMD 则在两天后推出了第六代 EPYC。 96 核 EPYC 9686F 更接近 Vera 的 88 核数量，提供 16 个内存通道，支持 DDR5-8000 或 MRDIMM-12800，每插槽速度为 1,024 或 1,638 GB/s，最高 MRDIMM 速度使 Venice 的理论带宽在总内存带宽和每核心内存带宽上都比 Vera 更高，具体取决于您所查看的 SKU。

新的 EPYC 规格和我们的 Turin 测试所展示的内容比 NVIDIA 声称的“内存带宽比最新 x86 CPU 高 3 倍”要窄，这取决于 Turin 结果，并不代表我们可以从同一代处理器中提取的带宽。 与我们的结果相比，Vera 提供了大约 1.9 倍的总带宽和 2.8 倍的每个核心带宽，这仍然是一个令人印象深刻的平台结果，但这并不能证明单片 Arm 处理器比基于小芯片的 x86 CPU 具有带宽优势。

NVIDIA 报告称，PageRank 比 EPYC 9755 提高了 2.6 倍，并显示 Vera 几乎可以线性扩展至 32 个核心，而 EPYC 在 32 个核心上性能仅提升 10 倍。 NVIDIA 将这一相对于 Turin 的改进归功于其高带宽可扩展一致性结构的单片计算芯片、Vera 的 1.2 TB/s 内存带宽以及 Olympus 核心内的图形预取器。

然而，虽然该论文链接了 GAP Benchmark Suite，但它忽略了 NVIDIA 使用的变量是影响该测试运行方式的重要因素。 即使机器每个插槽有 88 和 128 个核心，缩放图也会停止在 32 个核心处。 虽然 2.6 倍的结果很有趣，但如果没有 NVIDIA 使用的变量，结果可能无法重现。

对于 ClickHouse 测试，NVIDIA 直接链接到 Phoronix 的结果，其中 Vera 带领测试的处理器在 1 亿行数据集上进行了三遍。 由于未使用 9575F 结果，白皮书的 1.2x 图表仍然是选择性的，但外部测试人员以可识别的工作负载生成了基础结果。

然后我们看到图 24，“Vera 在 RL 训练中驱动器提高了 1.8 倍”，该图是一排已完成任务的小方块。 没有模型、环境、CPU/GPU 分配、框架、批量大小、功率测量、重复计数或误差线。 我们甚至不知道这些方块是否代表样本、步骤，或者 NVIDIA 总部的某些图块的随机布局。

这不是一个糟糕的基准，它根本就不是一个基准。

周围的文本解释了为什么更快的 CPU 可以通过更快的环境步骤来改进强化学习的推出，并且奖励计算可以更快地为加速器提供数据，但图 24 甚至没有假装对其进行测量。

45 页后，我对 Vera 的立场比我对 Vera 白皮书的立场更加积极。

Olympus 看起来像一个严肃的核心，具有 10 宽固定长度解码器、大型私有缓存、值预测、积极的分支处理、图形感知预取和单片 88 核芯片，所有这些选择都指向非常高性能的 CPU 核心。 内存设置也毫不逊色，LPDDR5X 子系统可提供高达 1.2 TB/s 的内存带宽，这对于需要内存带宽的服务器工作负载来说是非常喜欢的，而且早期的独立基准测试表明，该芯片至少可以兑现白皮书中所写的部分检查。

然而，该论文的竞争论点却更加站不住脚，它错误地描述了 x86 SMT，将可选的 NUMA 配置转变为默认负担，将标准 CPU 测试重新标记为代理工作负载，将 3% 的双插槽速率领先隐藏在 1.8 倍每核条后面，比较未定义的跨 ISA 计数器，将内存接口的胜利归因于单片美德，并将插图呈现为性能数据。

这些都不会导致 Vera 变慢，它只是让 NVIDIA 的证明比 NVIDIA Marketing 的散文更小。

下一轮 Vera 测试应该很简单。 为独立审阅者提供不受限制的生产硬件，以便我们可以发布频率、封装功率和墙上功率数据，以及测试空间多线程开/关结果，当然还可以在 Vera 上运行我们希望的任何基准/工作负载。 如果 Vera 正如其架构所暗示的那样好，那么这些测试将比将 x86 SMT 绘制为微小的两车道交通灯更有说服力。 从目前的情况来看，NVIDIA 的营销可能会损害 Vera 的声誉。 NVIDIA 已经在这里构建了足够的 CPU，它可以停止从营销渠道借用性能。
